summary:
Central Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the sources reviewed identify no provincial-level legal divergence. OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping of Indonesian laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people lists eight provinces with discriminatory regional regulations; Central Kalimantan is not among them. The province adds no separate criminal or regulatory layer of its own to the exposure a trans visitor already carries under national law.

No provincial enforcement action, police operation, prosecution or incident directed at trans or LGBTIQ people in Central Kalimantan appears in the sources reviewed. Absence from a list of discriminatory regulations is a legal finding only. It does not establish how provincial police, local officials or communities treat trans visitors in practice, and nothing in the sources reviewed addresses that question.
tangentialFactors:
OutRight Action International's mapping catalogues national laws and regional regulations together, so Central Kalimantan's absence from its eight-province list comes from a survey built to detect discriminatory provincial rules rather than from a general survey of Indonesian law. The mapping dates from 2022.

The province's absence from that list is the only finding specific to it; the remaining legal exposure a visitor faces in Central Kalimantan is set nationally.
localsOnly:
Residents of Central Kalimantan live under the same national framework as the rest of Indonesia. None of the eight discriminatory regional regulations catalogued by OutRight Action International in 2022 applies in the province, and no provincial regulation identified in the sources reviewed imposes additional restrictions on LGBTIQ people.

The mapping covers regulations that violate the rights of women as well as LGBTIQ people, so the province's absence from it applies to both categories.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Central Kalimantan has adopted a discriminatory provincial regulation since 2022 is unresolved. The only regional mapping in the sources reviewed predates that year, and no later provincial survey is available.

No reporting on provincial police conduct, prosecution practice, custodial treatment or violence against trans people in Central Kalimantan appears in the sources reviewed. No homicide or violence rate for the province is available, so no comparison with any trans-specific figure can be made.
